t.1.33.1: The Sūta said: Having heard that curse from his mother, Vāsuki, the best of serpents, pondered how this curse might not come to pass.
t.1.33.2: Then he took counsel together with all his brothers, Airāvata and the others, who were devoted to dharma.
t.1.33.3: This curse, just as it was pronounced, is known to you, O sinless ones; let us take counsel together and strive for release from that curse.
t.1.33.4: For all curses, indeed, there exists a counteraction; but for those cursed by their mother, O serpents, no release could be found.
t.1.33.5: Having heard that we were cursed thus in the very presence of the imperishable, immeasurable and true one, a trembling arises in my heart.
t.1.33.7: Therefore let us take counsel together here on how the well-being of all the serpents may come about, so that this time of ours may not slip away.
t.1.33.6: Surely this utter destruction of ours has been proclaimed, for that imperishable god did not restrain her as she was uttering the curse.
t.1.33.8: For by taking counsel together we may yet see a means of release, just as the gods of old found Agni, who was lost and lay hidden, gone into a cave.
t.1.33.9: So that that sacrifice of Janamejaya, which is for the destruction of the serpents, may not take place, or else may come to ruin.
t.1.33.10: Having said "So be it," all those sons of Kadrū, assembled there and skilled in counsel and understanding, then made a compact.
t.1.33.11: Some of the Nāgas there said, "Having become eminent brahmins, we shall beg of that Janamejaya, saying, 'Let there be no sacrifice of yours.'"
t.1.33.12: But other Nāgas there, who considered themselves learned, said: "We shall all become his highly esteemed counsellors."
t.1.33.14: That king, the best of the wise, knowing us to be highly esteemed, will surely ask us for the sake of the sacrifice; we shall say "No."
t.1.33.13: He will ask us for a firm decision on the purpose in all his affairs; then we shall offer our counsel in such a way that the sacrifice is called off.
t.1.33.15: Pointing out many dreadful evils, both in the hereafter and here, with arguments and with reasons, so that that sacrifice might not take place.
t.1.33.16: Or else, the preceptor who will be at that sacrifice, one versed in the procedure of the snake sacrifice and devoted to the welfare of the king's affairs, ...
t.1.33.17: Some serpent from among those that bite should go to him, and he will die; once he, the one who performs the sacrifice, is slain, that rite will not take place.
t.1.33.19: Then other serpents, righteous in spirit, counseled: "This is folly on your part; the killing of a brahmin is not good."
t.1.33.18: And whatever others of this priest will be experts in the snake sacrifice, all of them too we shall bite; thus it will be accomplished.
t.1.33.21: But other Nāgas said, "Becoming clouds accompanied by lightning, we shall extinguish the blazing Jātavedas with showers of rain."
t.1.33.20: For in misfortune the highest peace is the one rightly rooted in true dharma; the ascendancy of adharma would surely destroy the whole world.
t.1.33.22: Or else let other excellent serpents go by night and swiftly carry off the vessels of ladles from the heedless priests; thus there will be an obstacle.
t.1.33.23: Or else, at that sacrifice, let the serpents in hundreds and thousands bite all the people; thus terror will arise.
t.1.33.24: Or else let the serpents defile the prepared food with their own urine and excrement, which ruins all food.
t.1.33.26: But others there said, "Let us bring the king home while he is sporting in the water and bind him; thus that sacrifice would not take place."
t.1.33.25: But others there said, 'We shall become his officiating priests and obstruct the sacrifice, saying, "Let the fee be given!" And he, having come under our control, will do as we wish.'
t.1.33.28: This indeed is the final resolve, approved by all of us; or else, O king, whatever you think fit, let that be arranged quickly.
t.1.33.27: But other Nāgas there, doers of good deeds, said: “Let us seize him quickly and bite him; thus it will be accomplished. When he is dead, as he shall be, the root of our misfortunes will be cut off.”
t.1.33.29: Having spoken thus, they all looked toward Vāsuki, the lord of serpents. And Vāsuki, after reflecting, spoke to those serpents.
t.1.33.30: O serpents, this plan of yours is not considered a sound one to carry out; the plan of all you snakes does not please me.
t.1.33.31: But what should be arranged here that would be beneficial for you all? Over this I am sorely tormented, for both the merit and the fault rest upon me.
